name: Emeka Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior operator on the surface-mount line at an electronics plant on the edge of town. We build circuit boards for heating controls and a few for medical pumps. My line is a solder paste printer, three pick-and-place machines that put tiny parts on the boards faster than you can blink, then a reflow oven and an inspection camera. I set the jobs up, swap the reels of parts, and chase down why the camera keeps rejecting board 4,000-and-something.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the puzzle. When the camera says a part's crooked, is it the nozzle, the paste, the board, the reel? I use an AI chat tool every day now to read the machine logs with me, and it's made me twice as quick at finding faults. What wears me out is that the pay is low for what we do, honestly. Ruth's a nurse and earns more than me, and we still finish most months at zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, actually, because the useful bits are really useful. I'd tell the lads on the line to keep using the tools anyway. Online I'd probably post something about how the gains should go to workers, not shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much changes. I'd still be the guy who's quicker because he uses the tools. That might even help me get the shift manager job, which would mean about three hundred more a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing and push for that manager job. I'd write up how I use the AI to find faults and show it to the plant manager, so they see the value. And I'd keep paying into the union, because a small pay rise for everyone matters more than one for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little disappointed, maybe, which I know sounds odd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd hoped it would make the boring parts of everyone's job go away and give us shorter weeks. A four-day week, that's what I'd want. If it's just hype, the boring parts stay and so does the five-day week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you finish most months at zero. What would three hundred more a month change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd actually save something. Ruth and I would start a rainy-day pot, maybe fix the roof gutter that's been leaking on the back step for two winters. Small stuff, but small stuff is what we can't do now.

S0.say: I'd say it's a shame because the useful parts of AI are really useful. Online I'd post that the gains should go to workers, not shareholders.
S0.think: I think nothing much changes for me. I'd still be quicker because I use the tools, which might help me get the shift manager job.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools on the line and writes up how he uses them to find faults to show the plant manager. Goes for the shift manager job and stays in the union.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little disappointed that the boring parts of work wouldn't go away.
S0.quote: If it's just hype, the boring parts stay and so does the five-day week.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka is unusual in being disappointed by the calm scenario: he'd hoped AI would bring shorter weeks. He uses the tools daily and sees them as his edge. Even with very little money, his politics stay collective, putting a raise for everyone ahead of one for himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is our chance to make work better, if workers get a say. At the union I'd push for us to help choose the new machines and to get trained to run them. Online I'd share how my line already works with AI and nobody's been sacked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well out of it. My line already runs mostly by itself, and the people who understand both the machines and the AI are going to be needed. The ones I worry about are the packers and the hand-solder people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the robot maintenance certificate at the college, the one that takes a year of evenings. I'd ask the plant to pay half, and offer to train other operators in return. And I'd run lunchtime sessions showing people how I use the chat tool, because if everybody's skilled, they can't pick us off one by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, honestly. Excited, with a bit of guilt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Grace on hand-solder has been there twenty-two years and she's going to have a harder time than me. I'm excited about something that might hurt her. I'd want the union to make sure there's a place for her, maybe in quality checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd train other operators. Is that a trade you'd make for free?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for free, no. I'd ask for a trainer allowance, even fifty a week. But I'd do it either way, to be honest, because I'd rather they learn from me than from a consultant who's never smelled a reflow oven.

S1.say: I'd say this is a chance to make work better if workers get a say. I'd push the union for us to help choose new machines and be trained to run them.
S1.think: I think I'd do well, since people who understand both machines and AI will be needed. I worry about the packers and the hand-solder workers.
S1.do: Signs up for a year-long evening robot maintenance certificate and asks the plant to pay half. Runs lunchtime sessions teaching others the AI tools and pushes the union for a say in new machines.
S1.feel: Excited, with some guilt about coworkers who'll find it harder.
S1.quote: I'd rather they learn from me than from a consultant who's never smelled a reflow oven.
S1.fieldNote: Emeka sees Steady Disruption as his moment and moves first. His guilt about Grace on hand-solder is real and he turns it into a demand on the union. He frames teaching others as a way of protecting the whole floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public answer, fast: some kind of basic income, paid for by taxing the firms that own the machines. I'd say it at work, I'd say it at the union and I'd say it loud online. This isn't something one family can fix on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the skills I'm proud of would be worth a lot for about a year. Somebody has to install and tune all those new robots. After that, if the AI can do almost anything, it can tune itself. And I have less than a month saved, so a year's not much of a runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd try to get on the team that commissions the new robots, at our plant or anywhere nearby, and I'd take every overtime shift going. Every extra bit of money goes into savings or paying off the car loan. I'd also pick up weekend repair jobs, fixing boilers' control boards and such, while people still pay for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. I'd be too busy to sit in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a year of being useful isn't much runway. What happens in year two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's where my plan runs out. I'm hoping by then there's a public scheme, because otherwise it's Ruth's salary carrying us, and nurses might get robots too eventually. I don't have a clever answer for year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ada and Chidi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ada's eleven and already asks the chat tool about everything, so she'd get it. I'd tell her the machines are doing dad's work now and dad's helping set them up. Chidi's eight; he'd only want to know if he can see the robots.

S2.say: I'd say this needs a fast public answer, like a basic income paid for by taxing firms that own the machines. One family can't fix this alone.
S2.think: I think my skills would be valuable for about a year installing and tuning robots, then the AI tunes itself. With under a month saved, that's not much runway.
S2.do: Tries to join a team commissioning the new robots and takes every overtime shift. Puts extra money into savings and the car loan, picks up weekend control-board repair jobs, and campaigns for a basic income.
S2.feel: Anxious but too busy to sit in it.
S2.quote: Somebody has to install and tune all those new robots. After that, if the AI can do almost anything, it can tune itself.
S2.fieldNote: Emeka's adaptability buys him a clear first year in the fast scenario, but he openly says his plan runs out in year two. That gap is where his politics come in: he wants a basic income because he can see personal effort won't be enough. His partner's nursing job is the household's anchor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get this right, so let's not waste the first two arguing. Workers should get training and a share of the savings. I'd post about it and push the union to make it the main demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I think I can get ahead of it properly. I'd finish the maintenance certificate and maybe a programming course, so I'm one of the people who sets up the cells. I still think the end point is that the machines don't need me, but I'd have built some cushion first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one: the certificate, plus volunteering for every new automation project at the plant. I'd ask to move into the engineering team on a trial. By year two I'd want three months saved, which we've never had, and I'd use the AI tools to apply for jobs at the bigger plants an hour away, even if it means a longer drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than not. It's a race I think I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you'd train others. Does that still happen in the five-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even more. With five years, I'd push the union to set up a proper training scheme and offer to run it. It's better for me too: the more people who can work with the machines, the stronger our hand at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, I'm grabbing a year of work and hoping. With five, I can actually move up a step, save a bit, and see the end coming from a better place. It's the difference between running and jumping.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get this right if we don't waste the first two arguing. Workers should get training and a share of the savings.
S3.think: I think I can get ahead by finishing the maintenance certificate and a programming course to set up robot cells. The machines may not need me in the end, but I'd have some cushion first.
S3.do: Finishes the maintenance certificate in year one and volunteers for every automation project, asking for a trial in the engineering team. Aims for three months of savings by year two and applies to bigger plants an hour away.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful than not, like a race he can run.
S3.quote: It's the difference between running and jumping.
S3.fieldNote: The five-year version is where Emeka feels most in control, with a step-by-step plan. He keeps tying his own progress to the strength of the whole workforce. He still believes the end point means machines won't need him, but he wants to meet it with savings and skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan a fair change, like a shorter working week that spreads the work around and a basic income at the end. I'd say we should start now. I'd be the annoying one bringing it up at every union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is a career. I could become a robot technician, maybe an automation engineer, and do well for most of it. My real worry is the end. At fifty-three, if almost all work is gone, what do I do with the next thirty years?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start the certificate. Then I'd aim for an engineering job within three years, which might mean moving to the city where the bigger plants are. I'd also want Ada thinking about what she studies, maybe something about people and machines together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a thinking way. More curious than afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move to the city. What does Ruth say to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth would say, as long as there's a hospital, I'm fine. We'd have to rent at first, because selling the house here wouldn't buy much there. It's a big step on thin savings, but with ten years we could plan it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think you'd do with those thirty years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I genuinely don't know. Fix old radios, coach Chidi's football team, volunteer. It depends on whether there's money for people to live on. If there is, it might even be good. If not, it's a disaster.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to plan a fair change, like a shorter working week and a basic income at the end. I'd raise it at every union meeting.
S4.think: I think ten years is a whole career where I could become a robot technician or automation engineer. My worry is what I do with the thirty years after that at fifty-three.
S4.do: Starts the certificate this year and aims for an engineering job within three years. Plans a move to the city where bigger plants are, renting at first, and steers his daughter's studies toward people and machines.
S4.feel: Uneasy in a thinking way, more curious than afraid.
S4.quote: At fifty-three, if almost all work is gone, what do I do with the next thirty years?
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Emeka's worry moves from money to meaning. He plans a move to the city and a new career, and he's realistic that thin savings mean renting. He sees the end point as either good or a disaster depending entirely on whether there's public money for people to live on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not for the first year, I'd be busy, but for the second. What would help is a basic income or something like it that's ready before it's needed, not after. And a share of the profits from the machines going back to the towns that built them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd want, as opposed to what I'd fear. I'd want a three-day week and time with my kids. If the machines can do the work, that should be the prize, not the punishment.

headlineQuote: If the machines can do the work, that should be the prize, not the punishment.
portrait: Emeka Varga is a 43-year-old senior operator on a circuit-board line, who uses an AI chat tool every day to read machine logs and find faults. He's curious and quick, but on low pay with almost nothing saved, and his partner Ruth's nursing salary is the household's anchor. He's calm through the first two scenarios and sees Steady Disruption as a chance to retrain as a robot technician and teach others. AGI in 2 years makes him anxious because his useful skills would only buy him about a year, while 5 or 10 years let him plan a career step and even a move. His politics stay collective throughout: he wants a basic income and a shorter week funded by the firms that own the machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, especially the second year, when his skills would no longer be needed and his plan runs out.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income or similar support that's ready before it's needed, and a share of the profits from machines going back to the towns that built them.
